clinicalPearls: Rare autosomal recessive skeletal dysplasia whose name derives from the Greek for 'late', reflecting the hallmark markedly delayed epiphyseal and carpotarsal ossification (retarded skeletal maturation) — the opposite of the advanced bone age seen in Desbuquois dysplasia.

Presents at or before birth with severe micromelia — short limbs with disproportionately short hands and feet — together with relative macrocephaly, frontal bossing, a depressed nasal bridge, small anteverted nares and a long philtrum.

Characteristic radiographic combination: severe platyspondyly, extremely short and squared metacarpals and phalanges, concave metaphyseal cupping, and ossification profoundly delayed relative to gestational or chronological age.

Biallelic loss-of-function variants in INPPL1 (encoding the inositol polyphosphate 5-phosphatase SHIP2) underlie most cases; a subset of clinically typical patients lack INPPL1 variants, pointing to locus heterogeneity.
Renal phosphate wasting with hypophosphataemic, rickets-like bone changes may accompany the dysplasia, so bone biochemistry and renal tubular handling of phosphate deserve evaluation.
A narrow thorax with respiratory insufficiency is the leading cause of early death; airway and ventilatory planning are central to neonatal management.
Antenatal ultrasound may show short-limb dysplasia with a small chest and relative macrocephaly; the striking discrepancy between skeletal maturity and gestation is a diagnostic clue.
Intelligence is generally preserved in survivors, so prognostic counselling should separate the skeletal and respiratory burden from cognitive outcome.
reference.pathophysiology: Opsismodysplasia is most often caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in INPPL1, the gene encoding SHIP2 (SH2-domain-containing inositol polyphosphate 5-phosphatase 2), an enzyme that hydrolyses the 5-phosphate of phosphatidylinositol-3,4,5-trisphosphate and thereby dampens phosphoinositide signalling downstream of growth-factor and insulin receptors. Within the growth plate, disruption of this signalling is thought to impair chondrocyte proliferation and the orderly progression of endochondral ossification, generating the profound delay in epiphyseal and carpotarsal maturation, the metaphyseal cupping and the platyspondyly that define the disorder. SHIP2 also participates in phosphate homeostasis, which may account for the renal phosphate wasting and hypophosphataemic, rickets-like bone changes reported in some individuals. Because a proportion of clinically typical cases carry no identifiable INPPL1 variant, additional as-yet-undefined genetic causes are presumed.
additionalDifferentials: Desbuquois dysplasia (short-limb dysplasia but with advanced bone age and joint dislocations)
Short-limb spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia with hand anomalies
Achondrogenesis and other perinatally lethal short-limb dysplasias
Kniest dysplasia and spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia congenita
additionalInvestigations: Full skeletal survey with formal assessment of bone age and hand/foot morphology
Molecular testing of INPPL1 or a skeletal dysplasia gene panel, with parental testing
Serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase and parathyroid hormone
Renal tubular phosphate handling studies and urinalysis for phosphaturia
Renal tract ultrasound to look for nephrocalcinosis
Chest imaging and echocardiography to assess thoracic and cardiac status
Genetic counselling with discussion of autosomal recessive recurrence risk
redFlags: Progressive respiratory distress or failure from a small thorax in early infancy
Feeding difficulty with failure to thrive
Biochemical hypophosphataemia with clinical or radiographic rickets
reference.prognosis: Early mortality from respiratory failure is common in the neonatal and infant period; survivors have disproportionate short stature and may develop metabolic bone and renal complications, while cognition is usually preserved.
pitfalls: Interpreting the delayed ossification as a lethal achondrogenesis and withdrawing care prematurely
Overlooking treatable hypophosphataemia and renal phosphate wasting
Assuming dominant inheritance and understating the autosomal recessive recurrence risk
Attributing the short limbs to constitutional smallness rather than a defined dysplasia
references: International nosology and classification of genetic skeletal disorders
Standard clinical genetics and dysmorphology reference texts
